notes: TEXTBOOK: For 2026-27 CBSE Class IX moved to the NCF-SE 2023 scheme. NCERT's new book is 'Ganita Manjari' (Part I, chapters 1-8, digital release about mid-April 2026; Part II, chapters 9-14, first edition August 2026, posted on ncert.nic.in at the end of September 2026). The old rationalised 'Mathematics: Textbook for Class IX' is no longer the book. The CBSE curriculum still writes 'Mathematics - Textbook for class IX, NCERT' generically (it was published 2 April 2026, before Part II existed).

VERIFICATION: ncert.nic.in textbook pages and PDFs (iemh101-108, iemh201-206) are blocked to the fetch tool (robots), so I could not open the book itself. Part I chapter titles are verified from official NCERT sources (CIET audio-book page; NCERT library record for the book title). Part II chapter titles 9-14 come only from secondary sites (learnify.bh, extramarks, teachoo, odinnclasses, tiwariacademy), which all agree; marked verified:false.

TITLE WORDING: the CIET listing gives the Part I titles from audio file names, so its punctuation is unreliable. For Ch 5, the printed form 'I'm Up and Down, and Round and Round' (with comma) follows extramarks and edzy. For Ch 8, sources disagree between 'Progressions' and 'Progression'; 'Progressions' is used, as in CIET and most sources.

SECTIONS: Part I section titles come from secondary sites (edzy.ai topic inventories; teachoo for Ch 6 order and the Heron/Brahmagupta/circumcircle/squaring sections), not from the printed book. They match the official CBSE topic lists closely but wording may differ slightly from the print. Ch 3 headings follow edzy (main headings); teachoo shows finer sub-headings (number line, absolute value, rationals between rationals, construction of sqrt n, story of pi and Madhava's series, cyclic numbers, square-root spiral). Part II sections are left empty because no reliable list of printed headings was found.

MISMATCH CBSE vs TEXTBOOK: The CBSE 2026-27 curriculum (April 2026) lists 15 topic-chapters (Number System; Introduction to Polynomials; Sequences and Progressions; Exploring Algebraic Identities; Linear Equations in Two Variables; Coordinate Geometry; Introduction to Euclid's Geometry: Axioms and Postulates; Lines and Angles; Triangles - Congruence Theorems; 4-gons (Quadrilaterals); Circles; Area and Perimeter; Surface Area and Volume; Statistics; Introduction to Probability). Ganita Manjari has 14 chapters and NO separate chapters for Euclid's geometry, Lines and Angles or Triangle congruence; a secondary site reports NCERT saying (25 Sep 2026) that no topics were removed and that these ideas are spread over Chs 5, 6, 9, 12, 13. I put the CBSE-listed Euclid / lines-and-angles / congruence outcomes under Ch 9 (Propositions and their Converses, which proves the isosceles theorem and Pythagoras converse by congruence) and flagged them; their exact textbook location is unverified.

CH 11 'The World of Algorithms' (algorithms for addition, divisors, GCD by Euclid's subtraction/division algorithm, Aryabhata's division algorithm, primality and prime factorisation) has no matching chapter in the April 2026 CBSE curriculum; computational thinking is listed as an outcome in every CBSE chapter. Whether Ch 11 is examined in 2026-27 is unverified. A secondary site says CBSE was expected to issue a final 2026-27 syllabus in October 2026; I found no such revised document on cbseacademic.nic.in as of 2026-10-19.

CH 10 (data): CBSE lists weighted averages, stacked and 100% stacked bar graphs, and mean/median/mode for decisions. Secondary summaries of the chapter mention weighted means, mixtures and stacked charts but not median/mode; the mean/median/mode outcome follows CBSE.

CH 14: CBSE outcomes list cuboids, cubes, cylinders, cones, pyramids, spheres and hemispheres, while the CBSE topic line names only spheres, hemispheres and right circular cones. I followed the fuller outcome list (secondary chapter summaries agree).

CH 6: CBSE outcomes include Heron's formula, Brahmagupta's formula (Heron as special case), the classical squaring problem / Baudhayana, circle area, sector and segment area, arc length, and the history of pi. Segment area is in the CBSE outcomes; a secondary site places sector/segment problems in Exercise Set 6.3.

CH 3: CBSE requires the irrationality proofs for sqrt 2 and sqrt 3 and density of rationals. Secondary summaries of the chapter show an end-of-chapter proof for sqrt 5 and a proof that (a+b)/2 lies between a and b; the exact placement of the sqrt 2 / sqrt 3 proofs in the book is unverified.

ASSESSMENT (CBSE 2026-27): theory 80 marks, 3 hours; unit weights Number System 7, Algebra 20, Coordinate Geometry 4, Geometry 25, Mensuration 14, Statistics and Probability 10 (204 periods). Typology: Remembering/Understanding 43 (54%), Applying 19 (24%), Analysing/Evaluating/Creating 18 (22%). Internal assessment 20: pen-paper test and multiple assessment 10 (5+5), portfolio 5, lab practical 5 (activities from the prescribed lab books). Prescribed: NCERT textbook, CBSE Guidelines for Mathematics Laboratory Class IX, NCERT Laboratory Manual Secondary, NCERT Exemplar Class IX (Exemplar is still the old-book version; mismatch not resolved).

DELETED TOPICS: the CBSE document lists none. Compared with the old rationalised book, the new syllabus has no remainder/factor theorem, no laws of exponents for real numbers or rationalising denominators, and no separate Heron's chapter. New topics: sequences (AP/GP), probability, Brahmagupta, pairs of linear equations, algorithms, weighted mean, pyramids.

ADVANCED LEVEL: CBSE also publishes an optional 'Mathematics at Advanced Level' for Grade 9 (own CBSE text: Sets; Logarithms; Relations and Functions; Coordinate Geometry; Combinatorics; Exploring some more Progressions). This is out of scope and not included; who takes it and how it is assessed could not be confirmed.

MAPPING: several outcomes map to existing competencies whose grade band is 10 or 11 (e.g. MATH.algebra.arithmetic-sequences, MATH.algebra.geometric-sequences, MATH.algebra.linear-systems, MATH.number.euclid-algorithm, MATH.measurement.sectors, MATH.reasoning.logic) because the new Grade 9 book introduces them earlier; the competency grade ranges may need widening. MATH.algebra.factor-theorem and MATH.number.radicals (Grade 9 in v1) are not used: those topics are not in the 2026-27 Grade 9 syllabus.

chapters.title: Orienting Yourself: The Use of Coordinates

sections.title: Distance Between Two Points in the 2-D Plane

outcomes.statement: Locate and plot points in the 2-D Cartesian plane, using the signs of coordinates to name quadrants and points on the axes, and use a grid to describe a floor plan or map.
Find the distance between two points from their coordinates, explaining how the formula follows from the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem.
Find the midpoint of a segment from the coordinates of its endpoints and use it to locate missing points.
Use coordinate distances to decide whether three points are collinear or whether a triangle is right-angled or isosceles, and justify the conclusion.
Recognise polynomials among algebraic expressions and identify their terms, coefficients and degree, classifying linear polynomials.
Detect a constant difference in a table or pattern and write the linear polynomial rule that generates it.
Model situations of steady increase or decrease (linear growth and decay) with a linear polynomial and use it to predict values.
Read off and interpret the slope and y-intercept of y = ax + b from an equation, table or graph as rate of change and starting value.
Draw the graph of a linear relationship and compare relationships by their graphs.

sections.title: The Dawn of Mathematics: The Human Need to Count
The Revolution of Śhūnya: When Nothing Became Something
Filling the Spaces: Fractions and Rational Numbers
Real Numbers: Decimals and Cyclic Patterns

outcomes.statement: Classify numbers as natural, whole, integer, rational, irrational or real, and place rational numbers (including their absolute values) on the number line.
Find rational numbers between two given rationals and explain why there are infinitely many (density), e.g. by showing the average of two numbers lies between them.
Decide whether a rational number has a terminating or recurring decimal expansion, convert recurring decimals to p/q form, and explore cyclic patterns in such expansions.
Prove by contradiction that sqrt 2 and sqrt 3 are irrational.

proposed.name: Prove that a number is irrational
proposed.why: MATH.number.real-numbers covers representing and classifying rational/irrational numbers, not writing a proof by contradiction that a specific number (sqrt p, a + b sqrt p) is irrational, which CBSE assesses in Grades 9 and 10.

outcomes.statement: Construct segments of length sqrt n on the number line and draw the square-root spiral using right triangles.

proposed.name: Construct irrational lengths such as sqrt n on the number line
proposed.why: Locating sqrt n on a number line / building the square-root spiral with right triangles is a construction skill not covered by MATH.number.real-numbers or the Grade 6 construction competency.

outcomes.statement: Explain that pi is irrational and that real numbers have non-terminating non-recurring decimals when irrational, citing historical approaches such as Madhava's series.

sections.title: Factorisation of Algebraic Expressions Using Identities

outcomes.statement: Justify identities such as (a+b)^2, (a-b)^2, a^2-b^2 and (x+a)(x+b) with area models or algebra tiles.
Expand products using identities, including (a+b+c)^2 and cube identities, and use identities for quick numerical calculation.
Factorise expressions using identities, including difference of squares, perfect squares, sum and difference of cubes and a^3+b^3+c^3-3abc.
Factorise quadratic trinomials, first with algebra tiles and then by splitting the middle term.
Discover and verify new identities (e.g. difference of consecutive squares) and argue why they hold for all values.
Simplify rational algebraic expressions by factorising and cancelling common factors.

proposed.name: Simplify rational algebraic expressions
proposed.why: No existing competency covers cancelling common factors and combining algebraic fractions.

chapters.title: I'm Up and Down, and Round and Round

sections.title: Chords and the Angles They Subtend
Midpoints and Perpendicular Bisectors of Chords
Distance of Chords from the Centre

outcomes.statement: Use circle vocabulary (centre, radius, diameter, chord, arc, segment, sector) and describe a circle's symmetries.
Prove that exactly one circle passes through three non-collinear points and construct the circumcircle and circumcentre of a triangle.
Prove and apply that equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre (and the converse), and that the perpendicular from the centre bisects a chord (and the converse).
Prove and apply that equal chords are equidistant from the centre (and the converse) and that the longer of two chords is nearer the centre.

Prove that the angle an arc subtends at the centre is twice the angle at the remaining circle, and deduce that angles in the same segment are equal and the angle in a semicircle is a right angle; use these to find angles.
Decide when four points are concyclic and prove and apply that opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary, together with the converse.

sections.title: Perimeter of a Circle — The C/D Ratio
Length of an Arc of a Circle
Problems, Puzzles, and Paradoxes on Perimeter
Circumcircle and Incircle of a Triangle
Brahmagupta's Formula for the Area of a Cyclic 4-gon

outcomes.statement: Calculate perimeters of polygons and circles, explaining that circumference/diameter is the same constant pi for every circle and recalling historical approximations of pi.
Find the length of an arc from its central angle and the perimeter of a sector, in applied problems.

competencies.why: The perimeter of a sector (and arc length) is asked by aisector (b09, ask 2), in circle-area, which the outcome is not mapped to.

outcomes.statement: Calculate areas of rectangles, parallelograms and triangles and explain why a median divides a triangle into two triangles of equal area.

competencies.why: aipara asks the area (and perimeter) of a parallelogram from base and height, the missing part of this outcome.

outcomes.statement: Calculate the area of a triangle from its three sides using Heron's formula.
Use Brahmagupta's formula for the area of a cyclic quadrilateral and explain why Heron's formula is the special case with one side zero.

proposed.name: Find the area of a cyclic quadrilateral using Brahmagupta's formula
proposed.why: MATH.measurement.heron is triangle-only; Brahmagupta's formula for cyclic 4-gons (with Heron as the special case) is new in the Ganita Manjari/CBSE 2026-27 syllabus.

outcomes.statement: Explain and carry out the Sulbasutra construction that turns a rectangle into a square of equal area, justifying it.
Derive and use the area of a circle and the areas of a sector and a segment of a circle.

chapters.title: The Mathematics of Maybe: Introduction to Probability

sections.title: Experimental Probability: Performing Observations or Experiments
Elements of Probability: Sample Spaces and Events

outcomes.statement: Describe randomness and place events on a probability scale from impossible (0) to certain (1).
Estimate probabilities from experiments, observations or simulations as relative frequencies.
List the sample space of a random experiment and describe events as subsets of it.
Calculate theoretical probabilities of events when outcomes are equally likely.
Use tree diagrams and tables to list outcomes of two-stage experiments and find probabilities.

proposed.name: Use tree diagrams and two-way tables for compound experiments
proposed.why: MATH.probability.sample-space covers listing simple sample spaces; organising multi-stage outcomes with tree diagrams/tables is a separate representational skill named in the CBSE Grade 9 curriculum.

outcomes.statement: Compare experimental and theoretical probabilities and explain why they get closer as the number of trials grows.

chapters.title: Predicting What Comes Next: Exploring Sequences and Progressions

sections.title: Sum of the First n Natural Numbers

outcomes.statement: Spot patterns in sequences and predict further terms.

competencies.why: Grade 9 sequence patterns (multiplicative and mixed rules t(n+1) = r t(n) + d, two-term recursions) are asked by ahrec and ahfib, which belong to another competency.
Non-linear patterns (squares, triangular, cube and doubling numbers) with further terms predicted are affig.

outcomes.statement: Write explicit (nth-term) and recursive rules for a sequence, generate terms from either, and convert between them.

proposed.name: Describe sequences with explicit and recursive rules
proposed.why: Existing pattern competencies stop at describing rules in words; writing and converting between nth-term (explicit) and term-to-term (recursive) symbolic rules is not covered.

outcomes.statement: Identify arithmetic progressions, find the nth term, and relate an AP to a linear graph and to everyday contexts.
Derive and use the formula n(n+1)/2 for the sum of the first n natural numbers.
concepts: sum of first n natural numbers

outcomes.statement: Identify geometric progressions, find the nth term, and relate a GP to repeated growth or decay in context.
Apply GPs and recursive thinking to fractals and the Tower of Hanoi, e.g. finding the minimum number of moves.

proposed.name: Describe sequences with explicit and recursive rules
proposed.why: Existing pattern competencies stop at describing rules in words; writing and converting between nth-term (explicit) and term-to-term (recursive) symbolic rules is not covered.

outcomes.statement: Write a statement in if-then form, identify hypothesis and conclusion, form its converse and decide whether each is true.
Disprove a general claim with a counterexample, such as expressions that seem to always give primes.
Prove number-theory statements and their converses, e.g. on divisibility or that a number is a perfect square exactly when it has an odd number of factors.
Prove that the angles opposite equal sides of a triangle are equal, and the converse, using congruence.
Prove the converse of the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem by building a congruent right triangle (SSS).

Apply congruence conditions (SAS, ASA, AAS, SSS, RHS) to show triangles congruent and deduce equal parts, explaining why SSA is not a valid condition in general. [CBSE 'Triangles - Congruence Theorems'; textbook location unverified]

Use definitions, axioms and postulates, together with linear pairs, vertically opposite angles, angles made by a transversal with parallel lines and the triangle angle sum, as steps in deductive proofs, including proof by contradiction. [CBSE 'Euclid's Geometry' and 'Lines and Angles'; textbook location unverified]
Pose a statistical question, collect and organise data, and present it in a suitable table or graph.
Calculate weighted means and combined means of groups of unequal size, and say when an average of averages misleads.

proposed.name: Calculate and interpret weighted and combined means
proposed.why: MATH.statistics.averages-intro covers the simple mean; weighting values, combining group averages of unequal sizes and mixture concentrations is a distinct skill.

outcomes.statement: Find the concentration or price of a mixture from its parts, and how an average changes when values are added or removed.

proposed.name: Calculate and interpret weighted and combined means
proposed.why: MATH.statistics.averages-intro covers the simple mean; weighting values, combining group averages of unequal sizes and mixture concentrations is a distinct skill.

outcomes.statement: Read, construct and compare clustered, stacked and 100% stacked bar charts, telling absolute quantities apart from proportions.

proposed.name: Read and construct stacked and 100% stacked bar charts
proposed.why: Existing bar-chart competencies (Grades 3-4) do not cover comparing parts of wholes and absolute vs proportional quantities using clustered, stacked and 100% stacked bars.

outcomes.statement: Choose mean, median or mode to summarise data for a decision and justify the choice.
Describe an algorithm as a finite sequence of precise steps and trace standard column addition with carries, including with decimals, justifying each step by place value.

proposed.name: Describe, trace and improve step-by-step algorithms
proposed.why: No existing competency covers specifying an algorithm precisely, tracing it on inputs, and comparing or improving its efficiency (computational thinking stressed throughout the CBSE 2026-27 Grade 9 curriculum and Ganita Manjari Ch 11).

outcomes.statement: List the divisors of a number efficiently (testing only up to its square root) and use step-by-step procedures to test primality and find prime factorisations.

competencies.why: Step-by-step prime factorisation is assessed by ajpf (prime-factorisation competency), which the outcome is not mapped to.

proposed.name: Describe, trace and improve step-by-step algorithms
proposed.why: No existing competency covers specifying an algorithm precisely, tracing it on inputs, and comparing or improving its efficiency (computational thinking stressed throughout the CBSE 2026-27 Grade 9 curriculum and Ganita Manjari Ch 11).

outcomes.statement: Find the GCD (HCF) of two numbers with Euclid's subtraction and division algorithms and relate it to Aryabhata's division method.

competencies.why: Euclid's subtraction algorithm is akeuclid (where the repeated-subtraction game ends = the HCF); the outcome is mapped only to euclid-algorithm.

outcomes.statement: Find the LCM by listing multiples or from prime factorisations and relate it to the GCD.
Compare two algorithms for the same task by the number of steps they take, and improve one, using lists to keep track of intermediate data.

proposed.name: Describe, trace and improve step-by-step algorithms
proposed.why: No existing competency covers specifying an algorithm precisely, tracing it on inputs, and comparing or improving its efficiency (computational thinking stressed throughout the CBSE 2026-27 Grade 9 curriculum and Ganita Manjari Ch 11).

outcomes.statement: Define a 4-gon precisely, tell convex from non-convex quadrilaterals, and use the 360-degree angle sum.
Prove that in a parallelogram opposite sides and opposite angles are equal and the diagonals bisect each other.

competencies.why: The proof that the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other is the existing written task wr:tpf:diagonals in triangle-proof; no new content is needed.

proposed.name: Prove properties and tests of parallelograms
proposed.why: MATH.geometry.quadrilaterals (Grade 8) covers using angle properties; deductively proving parallelogram properties and their converses (tests) is not covered.

outcomes.statement: Prove and apply the tests for a parallelogram (converses of its properties, and one pair of opposite sides equal and parallel), and use them to find unknown sides and angles.

proposed.name: Prove properties and tests of parallelograms
proposed.why: MATH.geometry.quadrilaterals (Grade 8) covers using angle properties; deductively proving parallelogram properties and their converses (tests) is not covered.

outcomes.statement: Prove and apply the midpoint theorem and its converse.

proposed.name: Prove and apply the midpoint theorem and its converse
proposed.why: No existing competency names the midpoint theorem, its converse, and consequences (Varignon parallelogram, centroid dividing medians 2:1).

outcomes.statement: Prove that the medians of a triangle meet at a point that divides each in the ratio 2:1, and that joining the midpoints of any quadrilateral's sides gives a parallelogram.

proposed.name: Prove and apply the midpoint theorem and its converse
proposed.why: No existing competency names the midpoint theorem, its converse, and consequences (Varignon parallelogram, centroid dividing medians 2:1).

outcomes.statement: Use coordinates to find midpoints of diagonals and the missing fourth vertex of a parallelogram.
Describe the reflection, rotation and central symmetries of quadrilaterals and explain how copies of any quadrilateral tile the plane.
Write a linear equation in two variables for a situation and recognise that its solutions are ordered pairs, with infinitely many in general.
Draw the graph of a linear equation in two variables and use slope-intercept form to describe it.
Represent and interpret graphs when x and y can take only certain values (e.g. whole numbers in context).
Solve a pair of linear equations graphically and classify it as consistent (one or infinitely many solutions) or inconsistent from the lines.
Solve a pair of linear equations by substitution and by elimination.
Model word problems with a pair of linear equations, solve them and interpret the answer in context.

chapters.title: Math of Space: Surface Area and Volume

outcomes.statement: Calculate surface areas and volumes of cuboids and cubes, treating the cube as a special cuboid.
Calculate curved and total surface areas and volumes of right circular cylinders.
Find slant height, curved and total surface area and volume of right circular cones.
Calculate surface areas and volumes of spheres and hemispheres.
Calculate surface areas and volumes of pyramids with polygonal bases.

proposed.name: Calculate surface area and volume of pyramids
proposed.why: Existing solid-measure competencies cover cuboids, cylinders, cones and spheres but not pyramids, which the CBSE 2026-27 Grade 9 curriculum lists.

outcomes.statement: Estimate areas and volumes of real objects and explain how surface area and volume change as dimensions vary.
